worksheet.title: What Is a Bug?
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — read, find, and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find a bug in a loop and fix the repeat number.

parts.title: A bug is a mistake in code
text: A bug is a mistake that makes code do the wrong thing. Debugging is finding and fixing it.
Use 3 steps: say what the code SHOULD do, see what it DOES, then FIX the wrong part. Today the bug is the repeat number.

parts.caption: Debug in 3 steps: SHOULD → DOES → FIX.

parts.title: Bit should JUMP 5 times — but this is buggy
parts.note: It should be 5 jumps, but repeat 3 makes only 3. Fix the repeat number to 5.

parts.title: Find the bug
parts.prompt: Bit should CLAP 6 times. The code says repeat 4. What is wrong, and what should the repeat number be? ______

parts.title: Too many this time
parts.prompt: Bit should MOVE 4 times, but the code says repeat 7. Is that too many or too few? What should it be?

parts.title: Write the fix
parts.prompt: Bit should HOP 8 times. The code says repeat 2. Write the repeat number that fixes it:  repeat ______

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit should clap 6 times. The loop has TWO claps inside and says repeat 6 — so Bit claps 12! What repeat number gives exactly 6 claps? Explain.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To debug: say what the code SHOULD do, compare it to what it DOES, and change the wrong part. A wrong repeat number is the most common loop bug.

teacher_guide.title: What Is a Bug?
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 1. What Is a Bug — Teacher Guide

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students learn the debugging method — SHOULD, DOES, FIX — and apply it to find and fix a wrong repeat count in a loop (C3.2). The challenge separates total count from repeat count when two blocks are inside.

parts.title: Curriculum (Ontario Math 2020, Strand C3)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: A block-coding app (Scratch-style) to show a buggy loop and fix it live; the printed worksheet + a pencil per student.

parts.title: Run it (about 30 min)
text: 1. Define bug + debugging; introduce SHOULD → DOES → FIX with the jump example.
2. Run repeat 3 (3 jumps) vs the goal (5); fix to repeat 5 together.
3. Students do Exercises 1–4 (Ex 4 is the stretch), solo or in pairs.
4. Share answers; land the big idea: name the goal first, then find the wrong part.

parts.title: Answer key (checked by the run-gate)
text: Ex 2 — too many; should be repeat 4.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: not checking the goal first, so any number 'looks' fine.
Support: write the GOAL number, then compare to the repeat number.
Extend: ask the repeat for 10 claps with 2 inside (5).

parts.title: Success looks like
parts.text: The student states the goal, compares it to what the code does, and fixes the repeat number — including when two blocks inside change the total (Ex 4).
